newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish inflation to set another record in April.
newsitem.headline: Spanish inflation to set another record in April.

text.p: Wednesday's release of Spain's April inflation rate may come in even better than forecasts have suggested, perhaps beating the 1.9 percent average yearly rate predicted, economists said on Monday.
"There's a feeling the data may be slightly better than forecast, putting the inflation rate at lower than 1.9 percent," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
A monthly Reuters poll showed the April Consumer Price Index (CPI) was expected to add 0.23 percent from March to 1.9 percent year-on-year, versus a 29-year low of 2.2 percent the previous month.

Riccardo Barbieri, economist at Morgan Stanley in London, who was expecting inflation to fall to around 1.8 percent, said the fall would likely prompt the Bank of Spain to another 25 basis point rate cut.
"We expect the CPI to fall and the Bank of Spain to cut twice more, this month and the next. After that it's likely the Bank of Spain will hold its rate stable," said Barbieri.
Analysts' consensus showed the Spanish central bank could sanction its fourth easing this year by cutting 25 basis points to 5.25 percent as soon as Friday this week.
However some analysts said the direct link between an improvement in inflation and a rate cut was perhaps too obvious now.

"I don't know if (the central bank governor) Rojo likes to give the impression that each time inflation falls he's pushed the official money rate lower," said Yolanda Fernandez of Analistas Financieros Internacionales (AFI) .
Economists argued Spanish CPI could fall even further in May and then pick up slowly in the second part of the year.
"In May the CPI will fall to a minimum of 1.6 or 1.7 percent, then it will grow slowly toward two percent," said AFI's Fernandez.

Experts added that having benefited from a favourable comparison with the year-ago data, especially in food prices, it will be difficult for the CPI to show further declines in the second part of the year.
In the first part of 1996, the "mad cow" scandal pushed white meat prices higher, while olive oil prices were pulled down by an expectionally big harvest, experts remembered.
In the meantime swine fever outbreaks in the northwestern province of Lerida is expected to put pressure on pork prices.
More generally, economists expect a broad recovery of the Spanish economy will boost demand, making a further cooling down of inflation difficult.
BBV bank's economic department is expecting inflation to stabilise in May or June, ending 1997 below two percent.
"I think CPI wil remain below two percent given a good performance in processed food prices, while service prices will remain sticky," said Maite Ledo, economist at BBV in Madrid.
Ledo added private consumption, which seems to be growing at around 2.8 percent year on year versus 2.1 percent in 1996, is not pushing inflation higher.
